question: Does the Dayos case disclose a measured post-deployment error rate for automated Tier 1 tickets?
draft:
The available excerpts do not establish a measured post-deployment error rate for automated Tier 1 tickets.

**What the Dayos case does state about Tier 1**

Tier 1 tickets (60% of tickets; low severity, fully reversible — e.g. password resets, access requests, status inquiries) are fully automated by the agent using Simple Feedback, a propose-confirm loop, with no human engineer in the loop [4]. Every action produces a reasoning chain capturing classification logic and a confidence score, and a designated reviewer audits a cross-section of these biweekly [4]. The case states that because every Tier 1 action is reversible, errors can be corrected without lasting damage [4].

**Evidence gap**

The excerpts report a confidence score per action and a biweekly audit of a cross-section of reasoning chains [4], but they do not report any quantified error rate, error frequency, or measured post-deployment performance metric for Tier 1 automation. The only quantified figures in the Dayos excerpt relate to the ServiceNow retirement (45 days) and annual licensing savings ($121,000) [2].

child_citations.section_title: Dayos: Tiering and bounding agentic actions by risk level in IT management
child_citations.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
child_citations.quote:
Dayos: Tiering and bounding agentic actions by risk level in IT management

Dayos is an enterprise AI automation company headquartered in Singapore with operations in the US. The company builds Hero, an agentic platform that sits on top of Oracle, SAP, Workday, NetSuite and Microsoft Dynamics and automates workflows across IT management, accounting, HR and procurement.

Dayos replaced its own ServiceNow instance with an AI-powered ticketing agent built on Hero. The full retirement took 45 days and reduced legacy licensing costs by $121,000 annually. The agent now handles every internal IT request that comes in: it reads the ticket, determines how urgent and complex it is, and either resolves it automatically or routes it to a human.

Before any of this went live, Dayos ran a structured risk assessment. Every type of IT ticket was scored against three questions: • Severity of impact: If the agent gets this wrong, how bad is it? • Reversibility: Can the action be undone? • Feasibility of human oversight: Is it realistic for a human to review this at each step?

The scores determined which tier each ticket type falls into, and that tier dictated what reasoning strategy the agent uses and how much autonomy the agent gets.

What the agent does (and does not do) Tier 1 (60% of tickets)

Low severity, fully reversible

Password resets, access requests, status inquiries • Fully automated by agent using Simple Feedback (a propose-confirm loop). The agent proposes, the user confirms or pushes back, and agent adjusts until the ticket is closed. No human engineer is in the loop. • But with biweekly audits: Every action produces a reasoning chain that captures classification logic and a confidence score. A designated reviewer audits a cross- section of these biweekly. As every Tier 1 action is reversible, errors can be corrected without any lasting damage. Tier 2 (30% of tickets)

Moderate severity, partially reversible Chart of accounts updates, integration mapping corrections, diagnosing failed API connections • Agent diagnoses but can only act with a human engineer’s approval. Uses the ReACT strategy (a multi- step diagnostic loop for harder problems): the agent checks logs, queries connected systems, identifies the probable root cause, and writes up a diagnostic summary with a proposed fix. But a qualified engineer has to review and sign off before anything executes. Tier 3 (10% of tickets)

child_citations.section_title: Criterion 129: Monitor the system as agreed and specified in its operating
child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote:
Criterion 131: Monitor health of the system and infrastructure. This includes: o monitoring logs for errors

o services or processes o resources such as compute, memory, storage, and network. Criterion 132: Monitor safety. This includes: o monitoring inputs and outputs for abuse, misuse, sensitive information disclosure, and other forms of harm. Criterion 133: Monitor reliability metrics and mechanisms. This includes: o error rates o fault detection o recovery o redundancy o failover mechanisms. Criterion 134: Monitor human-machine collaboration. This includes: o reviewing the human experience o assessing the effectiveness of the human oversight and control measures o analysing the usage metrics for friction points and finding opportunities for improving the overall outcome from human-machine collaboration o considering different monitoring methods. While surveys could be cost effective, face-to-face interviews and observing users live while interacting with the AI system could provide better insights. Criterion 135: Monitor for unintended consequences. This typically includes: o implementing various channels for people to provide feedback, issues, or contest outcomes o consider if anonymous channels are needed o tracing how the outputs of the AI system are used o analysing quantitative and qualitative data for recurring harms

Periodically check that transparency and explainability requirements are met post deployment. Criterion 137: Monitor costs. The cost model for using AI systems may be different and much more costly than traditional software and systems. Criterion 138: Monitor security. This may include logging AI services in use to satisfy security requirements and ensuring appropriate data loss prevention (DLP). Identify the scope of deployment data for the AI system. These include: o data submitted by the user (prompts) o agency data augmented into the prompts o content generated by the service via completions, images, and embedding operations o training and validation data from the department that will be used for fine-tuning a model. DLP includes: o ensuring that the supplier does NOT use agency data for improving the supplier's AI systems or other products o ensuring the system only accesses data that the end user is authorised to access o ensuring that human review is performed by authorised users only o monitoring for sensitive data disclosure o monitoring data access and usage o automating data classification o monitoring for anomalies and suspicious activities o ensuring data encryption is enabled for data-at-rest and data-in-transit

child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote:
Disaggregating performance metrics into suitable attributes can detect whether a system performs fairly across demographics, environmental conditions, and other risk factors ◦ analyse data for bias and fix issues in the data.

See Model and Context dataset section for more information ◦ test independence strategy, functional performance testing, fairness testing, and user acceptance testing ◦ configure, calibrate, and monitor bias-related metrics during phased roll-out ◦ monitor bias-related metrics and unintended consequences during operations. Provide mechanisms for end users to report and escalate experiences of bias ◦ audit for how risks of bias are identified, assessed, and mitigated throughout the lifecycle ◦ find and use suitable tools that discover and test for unwarranted associations between the AI system outputs and protected input features

◦ implement bias mitigation techniques after harmful bias has been identified ◦ implement bias mitigation thresholds that can be configured post-deployment to ensure equity for cohorts, such as people with lived experience.
